title: Yonaguni Meaning: What Bad Bunny Says in Japanese at the End
excerpt: What does Bad Bunny say in Japanese at the end of Yonaguni? The 2021 single's meaning, the island it's named after, its English translation and the video.
content:
Yonaguni is about missing someone so badly that Bad Bunny would fly to the far end of Japan to find her, and the Japanese lines at the end are him telling her he wants only her tonight and asking where she is. Yonaguni is a real island, Japan’s westernmost, closer to Taiwan than to Tokyo, and in the song it stands for as far away as she could possibly be: por ti cojo un vuelo, for you I’d catch a flight. Bad Bunny released it as a standalone single on 4 June 2021.

The Japanese outro is what most people want explained. It is three short lines sung twice. The first says, bluntly, that he wants to sleep with someone today; the second, でもあなたとだけ (demo anata to dake), adds but only with you; the third, どこにいますか (doko ni imasu ka), asks where are you? After a song full of excuses, it is the most direct thing he says, and he says it in a language most of his audience couldn’t understand. That is the joke and the confession at once.

The rest of the lyric is a familiar weakness, written well. He knows he shouldn’t think about her, aunque sé que no debo pensar en ti, but when he drinks (pero cuando bebo) she is all he thinks about. If she gives him her address, he’ll send a thousand letters, si me das tu dirección, yo te mando mil cartas, an old-fashioned promise from a man who could just text.

Bad Bunny wrote it alone, and told Apple Music around the release that he had written it only about three weeks earlier, a quick snapshot of how he was feeling (we know this second-hand, through Songfacts). He described Yonaguni and 100 Millones, released a week apart, as a balance: one for the street, one chill and sweet to dance to in summer. Tainy, Smash David and FinesseGTB produced it, with Byrd also listed in the streaming credits. There is no credited sample.

Why that island? He hasn’t explained it, and according to Songfacts he had never been there. That fits the song: Yonaguni is a name on a map, a symbol of distance, and the town took it with some bemusement. In July 2021 local officials told the Okinawan paper Ryukyu Shimpo they were puzzled by the title, pointed out that the beach in the video didn’t appear to be theirs, and wondered if it might bring tourists.

The video, directed by Stillz, follows him trying and failing to get her off his mind. He eats sushi alone, walks dogs, tries martial arts and yoga, gets a Pokémon Go tattoo, goes to a party. None of it works. At the end he turns into an anime version of himself and sings the Japanese lines among cherry blossoms, which is where the song finally drops its guard.

It was huge straight away. Yonaguni debuted at No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot Latin Songs and stayed there for five weeks. It entered Streaming Songs at No. 2 with 27.3 million US streams in its first week and peaked at No. 10 on the Hot 100 and No. 3 on the Billboard Global 200. It is seven times platinum in Spain and platinum in Italy. In 2022 it was nominated for Best Reggaeton Performance at the Latin Grammys and Top Latin Song at the Billboard Music Awards, and it won an ASCAP Latin Award. It never made it on to an album, which makes it one of the biggest loose singles of his career. It is softer than the knowing flirt of Me Porto Bonito a year later, and a world away from the boasting of Monaco.

In March 2026 he finally sang it in Japan, at his first show there, near Tokyo. Before the song he told the crowd it was very special to him, and that when he made it he never imagined singing it there, with them. The crowd sang the Japanese lines back to him.

The island itself never made it into the video. It got the song instead.
